source.title: Strong Model Collapse
source.authors: Elvis Dohmatob; Yunzhen Feng; Arjun Subramonian; Julia Kempe

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some appendix references contain a placeholder, but this does not affect the reported results relevant to the claim.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports that synthetic-data mixtures can slow or plateau loss scaling, and that model-size effects can change across data regimes. These results qualify the scope of scaling-law claims.
record.gate_note: The GPT-2 and MNIST experiments report loss against token or sample count and varying synthetic-data proportions or model sizes. Figure-only values are recorded as such. Cited scaling-law results are not treated as this study's results. The theoretical linear-regression and random-projection analyses are not rows because they do not measure language-model pretraining loss or the image-model results cataloged here.
record.test_reason: The study trains GPT-2 on stories and MNIST networks on mixtures of real and synthetic data. It reports loss against tokens or samples and model size. It argues, and shows in its experiments, that non-vanishing synthetic fractions slow scaling and push it toward a plateau, and that larger models can do worse. This bears on whether loss scaling holds in another data regime (V5) and whether curves bend away from a single power law (V7).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that any non-vanishing synthetic fraction causes 'strong model collapse': larger training sets stop improving performance. Larger models can amplify collapse, but beyond the interpolation threshold they may mitigate it without preventing it. For GPT-2, the plateau is stated as an expectation, not an observed result; for MNIST, the plateau is stated as observed.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies synthetic-data mixtures and loss versus tokens, samples, or model size; it does not reproduce the original scaling-law measurement or fit the original parameter/token/compute laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Synthetic-data proportion and quality, model size, and sample or token count change the reported loss trends. The GPT-2 model-size curves change ordering across token-count regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory for linear and random-projection regression shows an extra error term of about p2^2 c2. Test error therefore plateaus unless the synthetic fraction vanishes. Confirmed on Gaussian toy data (Figs 3-5).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-data contamination with off-distribution (synthetic) data imposes a loss floor on data scaling, proportional to the squared contaminated fraction.

record.problems: Relevant loss values are shown only in figures, without numerical extraction in the text. The GPT-2 results use a small set of related models and a story dataset; the text frames eventual plateaus as expectations in some conditions rather than stating that they were observed. No power-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations are fitted.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant reported experimental conditions within the 60-row limit were omitted. The paper's theoretical classical-regression and random-projection results are not cataloged as rows because they are not language-model pretraining-loss measurements or image-model results.

untested.parts: Clean-data GPT-2 and MNIST curves are shown only as controls. No power-law fit or form is reported across parameters, tokens or compute.
Depth varies together with parameter count. No fixed-parameter shape test.
Video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested. No exponents are fitted in the synthetic regime.
Parameter counting, schedule, fitting method and published-law disagreement are not examined. Only data contamination is examined.

missing.what: Token thresholds for the GPT-2 size crossover: larger models better below 1e10 tokens, worse above 3e10 tokens.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Impact of Model Size; Figure 8 right

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed because contaminated-data runs are not V1's clean setting, and the clean controls report no fitted form. Size-comparison reference rows (r12, r35) were set to none. GPT-2 depth changes come with parameter changes, so they do not bear on V4. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Tests GPT-2 loss versus tokens in synthetic-data settings, not the general power-law relationship across parameters, tokens, and compute when other quantities are not bottlenecks.
No small-run fits are used to predict much larger runs.
No compute-budget allocation between parameter count and token count is optimized.
Models with different depths are compared at different parameter counts; depth, width, or architecture effects at a fixed parameter count are not tested.
Tests synthetic-data training with GPT-2 on stories and MNIST experiments. Does not test video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Shows sensitivity to synthetic-data proportion and model size, but does not fit or compare exponents, test parameter-counting or fitting-method choices, or evaluate compute-optimal splits.

labels.reason: MNIST plateaus and GPT-2 size-ranking crossovers support setup-dependent departures from uniform scaling. The reason overstates r3-r11: their eventual GPT-2 plateaus are predicted, not observed. Fitted exponents and compute-optimal splits are untested.

relation.reason: The study measures loss against sample count, token count, synthetic fraction and model size, and analyzes departures from scaling laws.

tranche.reason: Theoretical error floors and empirical scaling failures directly qualify power-law generalization to synthetic-data training.
